The bell curve, everywhere

Add up enough small, independent nudges and the same curve appears: in sample averages, in price bands, in risk models. Follow it across four fields, then see where it stops being true.

Regression to the mean

Extreme results tend to be followed by less extreme ones. It looks like a force pulling things back, but it follows from how averages work. Watch the same idea turn into trading signals, portfolio rules and model penalties.

Signal in the noise

Every field has the same problem: real structure mixed with randomness. These stops are the tools for pulling them apart, and for checking you have not invented a pattern that was never there.

Feedback loops

When a system's output feeds back into its input, small nudges can snowball. Crowds, prices, volatility and even deployed models run on loops like this, and they tend to stay quiet until they don't.

Survivors and false patterns

The data you can see is often the data that survived. Patterns found in it can be an artefact of what went missing. These stops show how the trap works, and the habits that keep you out of it.

Momentum

Recent direction tends to carry on, for a while. The same idea speeds up neural-network training, drives a family of trading indicators, shapes how traders add to winners and fuels the crowd. Follow it, and see where it stops paying.

Thresholds and tipping points

Many systems change all at once when a line is crossed. A neuron fires, a classifier says yes, a language model drops its unlikely words, a price breaks out, a stop-loss sells. Each stop is a threshold, and each has to answer the same question: where to draw the line.
